patterns.comment: The statement separator. A line break is the ordinary terminator in Lyra; `;` is the explicit form, for putting several statements on one line. The same token also separates the clauses of a C-style `for i = 0; i < n; i += 1` and the parts of an array repeat `[value; count]` — one scope for all three, as C and JavaScript grammars do.
patterns.name: punctuation.terminator.statement.lyra

patterns.comment: A divider rule (four or more slashes) is an ordinary comment, not documentation. It must come FIRST: `///.*$` would otherwise match `////////` and paint a section rule as a doc comment — the same reading the tree-sitter grammar goes out of its way to refuse (see include/comments.js, where `comment` outbids `doc_comment` at prec 2 for exactly this input).
patterns.name: comment.line.double-slash.lyra

patterns.comment: `///` documents the declaration below it and `//!` documents the enclosing module. Both are comment.line.documentation, which is the scope themes style as documentation; the two differ in what they attach to, not in how they read.
patterns.name: comment.line.documentation.lyra

patterns.comment: The `type` of a type alias (`type Op = ((i64, i64)) -> i64`). Kept out of the list above and gated on a following PascalCase name because `type` is NOT reserved in Lyra — the tree-sitter grammar makes it a keyword only in this position, so `let type = 5` is a legal binding and must not be painted as a keyword. An alias always names an uppercase type, so the lookahead separates the two with no false positives.
patterns.name: keyword.other.type.lyra

patterns.comment: The writable primitive types, from tree-sitter-lyra's _primitive_type. Removed 07/31: `int`/`uint`, which the language dropped for determinism (a platform-dependent width defeats the point), `float`, which is not a keyword — the sized f16/f32/f64 are — and `Void`, which is spelled lowercase. Added: i128/u128 and `rune`. Deliberately absent: `never`, the bottom type, which is compiler-internal and has no syntax to highlight.
patterns.name: storage.type.lyra

patterns.comment: The escape set is the grammar's, and the two must be kept together: tree-sitter-lyra's include/literals/char.js for runes, and pkg/analyzer/collector/expressions/string_literal.go's unescapeStringContent for strings — one decoder serves both. This rule had drifted, matching only [nrtfb\\"'] and so leaving \a, \e, \v, \oNNN and \# unpainted; \0 (NUL, 08/30) is added here rather than to a list that was already short.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.lyra

embedded-glsl.comment: A raw string marked /* glsl */ is GLSL (tree-sitter-lyra's queries/injections.scm is the same rule). It must be listed ahead of #comments: both start at the /*, and TextMate gives a tie to the first rule. The closer repeats the opener's # count through the \3 back-reference. The marker and the string must share a line — a TextMate begin cannot span two. The content is painted by syntaxes/glsl.tmLanguage.json, bundled under the private scope source.glsl.lyra.

regex-literals.comment: A regex literal is `r"…"` (tree-sitter-lyra's regex_literal). It was `r/…/` until 07/29, and this rule kept matching that long after: `let ratio = r/2 + a/b` painted a string from `r/` to the next `/`, which is exactly the lexical ambiguity the language change removed — a slash-delimited form cannot be told from division without arbitrarily distant context. A single `match` rather than begin/end, so the scope is bounded to one line: an unterminated literal must degrade to a stray identifier, never swallow the rest of the file. The alternation is the standard escape-aware string body, so `\"` does not end it.
regex-literals.name: string.regexp.lyra

patterns.comment: The four end operators: ..< ..<= ascend, ..> ..>= descend. The operator is a separate token after `..` in the grammar, so it is optional here too — a bare `..` is the open-ended form (`range(0..)`, the pattern `10..`). Longer alternatives first, or ..<= would match as ..< plus a stray =. Must stay ahead of the comparison rule so the < is not painted as a comparison; it already is, since this matches at the earlier `.`.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.range.lyra

patterns.comment: Shifts, split out from the bitwise rule below so they can sit AHEAD of comparison — otherwise a single < wins the tie at the same position and << paints as two comparisons. It cannot simply be the whole bitwise rule moved up: | would then beat the logical || the same way. Compound <<= / >>= are matched by the first rule in this list, which outranks both. Cost: the >> closing a nested generic (Maybe<Result<i64, string>>) paints as a shift — unavoidable without a parser, and it painted as two comparisons before.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.shift.lyra

patterns.comment: Bitwise or and xor. Must stay AFTER the logical rule so || is not split into two |. The shifts cannot live here for the mirror-image reason — see the shift rule above comparison. Bitwise & is left to the address-of rule below — same character, and both render as an operator. Xor is ~, which doubles as the prefix complement.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.bitwise.lyra
